prompt.context_jp: 都心の静けさに沈む安田邸の別邸のような重厚な玄関に、街灯の光___濡れた石畳を照らしていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces the streetlamp light as a new visual element setting the opening scene.

feedback.correct_en: This is a scene-setting opening: the light is newly introduced information painting the picture, so が is natural.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would imply the streetlamp light is an already-established topic, which doesn't fit the opening description. を marks an object, not the subject doing the illuminating.

contrast_examples.en: It's raining. (fresh observation — が)
The rain has stopped. (already-known topic — は)

prompt.context_jp: 明日の頭取就任挨拶へ向け発声を続ける男の声___、屋敷の奥からくぐもって漏れてくる。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces a newly-perceived sound in the scene.

feedback.correct_en: The voice is a new sensory detail entering the scene — perceived for the first time — so が marks it.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the voice as an already-established topic. で doesn't mark the subject of 漏れる here.

contrast_examples.en: I hear a sound. (newly noticed — が)
That sound has already stopped. (known topic — は)

prompt.context_jp: 安田___ソファから立ち上がり、酔いにもつれる足でリビングを横切ろうとしていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Yasuda is already the known figure in this scene. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: Yasuda has already been established in the chapter; the narration continues with him as the topic, so は is natural.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would suggest he's being newly identified as the one standing up, as if answering 'who stood up?' — not the case here.

contrast_examples.en: Yasuda (as topic) stood up.
It was Yasuda who stood up. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 書斎で抽斗をひとつずつ探っていた五月___、廊下から迫る足音を察して息を止めた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that marks May as the topic of this descriptive sentence.

feedback.correct_en: May has already been introduced and the sentence describes what she does — は marks her as the ongoing topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: が here would single her out as new information (answering 'who held their breath?'), which the narrative flow doesn't call for.

contrast_examples.en: May held her breath. (topic continuation)
It was May who held her breath. (identification)

prompt.context_jp: 何十分も探しつづけて、証拠らしきもの___まだ影も形もない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that highlights the absence of 'evidence' as the focal, contrasted point.

feedback.correct_en: は contrasts 'evidence' with everything else searched — many drawers opened, but evidence specifically is nowhere to be seen.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 'evidence' plain new info, losing the contrastive nuance of 'as for evidence, there's nothing.' も would mean 'even evidence,' which doesn't fit.

contrast_examples.jp: お金はないけど時間はある。
contrast_examples.en: I have no money, but I do have time. (contrastive は)
There's no evidence. (flat statement)

prompt.context_jp: 七菜のイヤホン越しの声___、細い糸のように五月を室内につないでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that presents Nana's voice as new information in the scene.

feedback.correct_en: The voice through the earphones is being newly introduced as a concrete image — it 'came in' as new info, so が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make it the topic, but it's a fresh sensory image here, not something already being discussed.

contrast_examples.en: The phone rang. (sudden event — が)
The phone won't ring anymore. (about the phone as topic)

prompt.context_jp: 書斎の扉まであと数歩というところで、千代___素早く回り込み、安田の袖に指をかけた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle marking Chiyo as the ongoing topic of her action.

feedback.correct_en: Chiyo is a known player; the sentence describes what she does next, so は flows naturally.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would feel like we're identifying 'who circled around' as if it were a mystery — but Chiyo's role is already clear.

contrast_examples.en: Chiyo (as topic) circled around.
It was Chiyo who circled around. (contrastive identification)

prompt.context_jp: 扉に手をかけた安田___、その動きをふと止めた。
prompt.prompt_en: After a relative clause 'Yasuda who had his hand on the door,' which particle fits the subject of 'suddenly stopped'?

feedback.correct_en: The relative-clause description sets up 'Yasuda who had his hand on the door,' and we report his action as a fresh event — が is natural.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would awkwardly re-topic a newly-described version of him. Here the narrative reports a sudden event, best with が.

contrast_examples.jp: 手をかけた男が、動きを止めた。
contrast_examples.en: The man who had put his hand on it suddenly stopped. (event focus — が)
Yasuda stopped his movement. (general topic statement)

prompt.context_jp: 千代___少し離れた位置から、その背中に貼りついた迷いを見逃さないでいる。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that keeps Chiyo as the discourse topic.

feedback.correct_en: Chiyo's perspective is being described as ongoing narration — は is used to keep her as the known topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would single her out, as if identifying who is watching — but the scene continues naturally about her.

contrast_examples.en: Chiyo was watching. (topic)
It was Chiyo who was watching. (identifying answer)

prompt.context_jp: 安田___結局 気配を追うのをやめ、ソファに深く沈み込んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for Yasuda who continues as the sentence's topic.

feedback.correct_en: The narrative continues to tell us about Yasuda's choice — he's the established topic, so は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would imply new identification, which doesn't match this quiet, resigned moment that summarizes Yasuda's behavior.

contrast_examples.en: In the end, he gave up. (topic continuation)
In the end, he (not someone else) gave up.

prompt.context_jp: 追い詰められているのは、こちら側だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 追い詰められているの___、こちら側だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that sets up the cleft 'the one being cornered was us.'

feedback.correct_en: In an 'XのはYだ' cleft, は marks the known presupposition ('the one being cornered') and the new, emphasized info comes after.
feedback.incorrect_en: が here would make the clause itself new info, breaking the cleft pattern. The sentence is specifically identifying who, which needs は + だ.

contrast_examples.en: The one at fault is me. (cleft with は)
I'm at fault. (plain identification)

prompt.context_jp: 生きろと言われることが、時にひどく痛いのだと、彼だけ___知っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: With 彼だけ ('only he'), which particle gives the exhaustive 'he alone knew' reading?

feedback.correct_en: 〜だけが emphasizes exhaustive listing: he, and no one else, knew this. が locks in that exclusivity.
feedback.incorrect_en: 彼だけは would shift to contrastive 'as for only him,' weakening the exclusive-subject reading. に doesn't fit the subject role here.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼だけが真実を知っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Only he knew the truth. (exclusive subject)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼だけは行かなかった。
contrast_examples.en: He alone didn't go. (contrastive)

prompt.context_jp: そこに、思いがけない小柄な影___立っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: A figure is suddenly discovered in the scene. Which particle introduces it?

feedback.correct_en: An unexpected figure is newly encountered — classic 'existence/appearance' context for が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose the figure is already known, contradicting 思いがけない ('unexpected'). で doesn't fit this existential pattern.

contrast_examples.jp: そこに人が立っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Someone was standing there. (new discovery — が)

contrast_examples.jp: その人はそこに立っていた。
contrast_examples.en: That person was standing there. (already-known topic)

prompt.context_jp: そのコートの裾___、千代の目に妙にひっかかった。
prompt.prompt_en: The coat's hem suddenly catches Chiyo's eye. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: It's a sudden perception — the hem catches her eye as a new, striking detail. が marks that spontaneous noticing.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make the hem a general topic for discussion, but the sentence is about the moment of noticing — が is right.

contrast_examples.en: Something caught my eye. (sudden perception — が)

contrast_examples.jp: そのコートは高かった。
contrast_examples.en: That coat was expensive. (topic は)

prompt.context_jp: 頭取室に置かれていた物ではないことは、彼女の勘___すぐに教えてくれた。
prompt.prompt_en: What tells her it wasn't from the president's office? Her intuition — and nothing else. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: The sentence spotlights her intuition as the specific thing that told her — が highlights this subject as the answer to 'what told her?'
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make 勘 just a general topic, losing the pointed 'it was her intuition that told her' feel.

contrast_examples.jp: 直感が答えを教えてくれた。
contrast_examples.en: Intuition told me the answer. (が identifies the agent)
Intuition is important. (general topic は)

prompt.context_jp: 前列の安田の顔からは、血の色___音もなく引いていく。
prompt.prompt_en: 'The color drained from his face.' Which particle introduces 血の色 as the thing being drained?

feedback.correct_en: This is a vivid, event-like description: the color of his blood drains — presented as observed new info via が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make 血の色 a discussed topic (unnatural here). を would require a transitive verb; 引いていく here is intransitive 'recede.'

contrast_examples.jp: 顔から血の気が引いた。
contrast_examples.en: The color drained from his face. (が for the fresh observation)
Blood color is red. (general topic は)

prompt.context_jp: 絨毯___踏むそのたびに、彼はほんの少しびっこを引くような歩みを見せる。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that marks the carpet as the direct object of 踏む (to step on).

feedback.correct_en: 踏む takes を for what is being stepped on. 絨毯を踏む = 'step on the carpet.'
feedback.incorrect_en: に would suggest a destination, and で would mark a location of action — neither captures the 'what is trodden on' meaning.

contrast_examples.en: Step on the floor.
Stand on the floor. (location target with に)

prompt.context_jp: 何十分も探しつづけて、証拠らしきものはまだ___もない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the set phrase meaning 'not a trace, not a shadow' — i.e., absolutely no sign.

feedback.correct_en: 影も形もない is a fixed idiom meaning 'nowhere to be seen, not a trace of it.' It fits the search turning up nothing.
feedback.incorrect_en: The other options aren't established idioms meaning 'no sign at all.' Only 影も形もない carries that nuance.

contrast_examples.en: There's no sign of the culprit at all.

contrast_examples.jp: 手がかりがまったくない。
contrast_examples.en: There are no clues whatsoever. (plain)

prompt.context_jp: 「___か…」(千代が両手で顔を覆う。)
prompt.prompt_en: Which four-character idiom means 'all options are exhausted / it's hopeless'?

feedback.correct_en: 万事休す means 'all is lost / nothing more can be done' — exactly Chiyo's despair after the failed search.
feedback.incorrect_en: 一期一会 is about cherishing a once-in-a-lifetime encounter; 七転八倒 describes writhing in pain. Neither fits 'we're doomed.'

contrast_examples.en: It's hopeless; let's give up.
A once-in-a-lifetime encounter.

prompt.context_jp: 「一原頭取が長年にわたり ___され ここまで成長してきた東都銀行の…」
prompt.prompt_en: Which four-character idiom means 'working one's bones to dust' — tireless, utmost effort?

feedback.correct_en: 粉骨砕身 (lit. 'pulverize bones, crush body') is a formal idiom meaning devoted, all-out effort — fitting for praising the former president.
feedback.incorrect_en: 一石二鳥 is 'two birds with one stone'; 朝令暮改 is 'constantly changing orders.' Neither conveys devoted service.

contrast_examples.jp: 粉骨砕身、努めてまいります。
contrast_examples.en: I will devote myself with all my might. (formal)
A two-birds-with-one-stone plan.

prompt.context_jp: 「地べた___でも… 生きててよ！」
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb completes 'even crawling on the ground, please stay alive'?

feedback.correct_en: 地べたを這いつくばる = 'crawl on the ground,' a vivid expression for enduring the worst humiliation to stay alive.
feedback.incorrect_en: 'Running around' or 'leaping up' don't match the sense of humble, desperate survival the line calls for.

contrast_examples.jp: 地べたに這いつくばる。
contrast_examples.en: Crawl flat on the ground.
Run around desperately. (different image)

prompt.context_jp: 「“そして ___の 傲慢な権力者のものでもない”」
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrase means 'a mere handful of' (people)?

feedback.correct_en: ひと握り literally 'one grip' / 'a handful' — standard idiom for 'a tiny minority,' fitting 'arrogant power-holders.'
feedback.incorrect_en: ひと押し means 'one push' (effort); ひと言 means 'a single word' — neither describes a small group of people.

contrast_examples.en: A handful of wealthy elites.
Just one more push. (different idiom)

prompt.context_jp: 「そもそも 年寄りが 道を___から こんなことになったんだ！」
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb forms the idiom 'won't yield / won't make way' in Yasuda's angry outburst?

feedback.correct_en: 道を譲る = 'give way / yield one's place.' With ない, it's Yasuda's accusation that the elderly 'won't step aside.'
feedback.incorrect_en: The other verbs don't collocate with 道を in the sense of yielding a position or role.

contrast_examples.en: Make way for the next generation.
Search for a path. (literal)

prompt.context_jp: 入れ違いに、初老の男性がひとり、___頭を下げながら小さな包みを差し出した。
prompt.prompt_en: Which adverb collocates with 頭を下げる to mean 'bow deeply'?

feedback.correct_en: 深々と頭を下げる is a fixed collocation for bowing deeply in gratitude or apology — fits the grateful man.
feedback.incorrect_en: 軽々と = effortlessly (used for lifting); ゆらゆらと = swaying. Neither matches a respectful, deep bow.

contrast_examples.en: He bowed deeply.
He lifted it effortlessly.

prompt.context_jp: 借金取りに追われ続けた兄の頬は___、影のような笑みだけが残っている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb describes cheeks becoming hollow/sunken from hardship?

feedback.correct_en: 頬がこける ('cheeks become hollow/sunken') is the standard expression for a gaunt, worn face.
feedback.incorrect_en: ふくらむ (swell) and のびる (stretch) would describe the opposite or something unrelated, not emaciation.

contrast_examples.en: His cheeks grew hollow from exhaustion.
His cheeks puffed up.

prompt.context_jp: Yasuda stood up drunkenly from the sofa. Which phrasing sounds most natural in Japanese narration?
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the most natural version of 'with unsteady, drunken feet.'

choices.text: 酔いにもつれる足でリビングを横切ろうとしていた。
酔いがもつれた足でリビングを横切ろうとしていた。
酔いでもつれた足のリビングを横切ろうとしていた。

feedback.correct_en: 酔いにもつれる足 ('feet tangled by the drunkenness') is the natural collocation — に marks the cause the feet are reacting to.
feedback.incorrect_en: B swaps subjects awkwardly (as if 酔い itself became tangled). C misuses の instead of で, breaking the modifying structure.

contrast_examples.en: Feet unsteady from fatigue. (natural pattern)
Eyelids growing heavy from sleepiness.

prompt.context_jp: At his inauguration, Yasuda introduces himself formally. Which version sounds most natural as a business greeting?
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the natural polite phrasing.

choices.text: 頭取の大役を仰せつかることになりました、安田英司でございます。
頭取の大役を命じられた安田英司だよ。
頭取の大役を仰せつかっちゃった安田英司です。

feedback.correct_en: 仰せつかる (humble 'to be entrusted with') + ございます is the standard register for inauguration speeches.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses casual だよ, inappropriate for a formal speech. C's ちゃった is too colloquial and undermines humility.

contrast_examples.jp: お役目を仰せつかりました。
contrast_examples.en: I have been entrusted with this duty. (formal humble)
I got asked to do it. (casual)

prompt.context_jp: Chiyo thinks: 'one more push and this man will choose sleep over doubt.' Which version is most natural?
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the natural phrasing.

choices.text: もう一押しあれば、この男は疑いよりも眠気を選ぶだろう。
もう一押しあれば、この男は眠気より疑いを選ぶだろう。
もう一押しあったら、この男が疑いを眠気より選んだろう。

feedback.correct_en: The logical meaning requires 'choose sleep over doubt' — i.e., give in to sleepiness. The AよりもB選ぶ frame ('choose B over A') puts sleep as what he picks.
feedback.incorrect_en: B reverses the meaning (he'd choose doubt). C garbles the particle pattern and tense.

contrast_examples.en: Choose family over work.
Choose work over family. (opposite)

prompt.context_jp: A reflective narrator line about saving someone's life. Which phrasing is most natural?
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the most natural version.

choices.text: 誰かの人生を救えるかどうかは、いつだって明日の朝には間に合わない。
誰かの人生を救えるかどうかが、いつだって明日の朝には間に合わない。
誰かの人生を救えるかどうかは、いつだって明日の朝で間に合わない。

feedback.correct_en: 〜かどうかは marks the whole clause as topic, and 〜に間に合う uses に for the deadline. This flows naturally as narration.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses が where the clause should be a topic — awkward. C replaces に with で, which doesn't fit 間に合う's deadline-marker.

contrast_examples.en: Make it in time for the deadline.

contrast_examples.jp: 電車に間に合わなかった。
contrast_examples.en: Didn't make the train on time.

prompt.context_jp: Yasuda says with dark humor that he's glad he waited without dying. Which sounds most natural?
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the most natural phrasing.

choices.text: 10日間 死なずに待ってて良かった。
10日間 死なないで待てて良かった。
10日間 死なずで待っていて良かった。

feedback.correct_en: 死なずに ('without dying') + 待ってて良かった ('glad I was waiting') is the natural idiomatic combination — 〜ずに expresses 'without doing.'
feedback.incorrect_en: B shifts to 死なないで 待てて (potential form), which sounds odd — he's not boasting of ability. C uses 死なずで, an ungrammatical particle combo.

contrast_examples.en: Left without saying anything.
Went to bed without eating.
